# Preface {.unnumbered}

Modern system and chip design asks architects to connect workloads, software,
architecture, RTL, physical implementation, verification, and product
constraints. AI can help with parts of that work. It can generate artifacts,
predict expensive results, choose which designs to evaluate, operate tools, and
organize findings. It can also preserve a bad assumption, optimize an incomplete
objective, or produce a confident explanation that the measurements do not
support.

> **Architecture 2.0.** Architecture 2.0 is the practice of using AI across
> system and chip design while keeping the architecture question, current
> design state, credible alternatives, physical consequences, evidence limits,
> and responsibility for the decision explicit.

The architecture problem comes first. A project may need a generator,
predictor, optimizer, critic, verifier, conventional analysis, or no AI at all.
The right choice depends on which work is limiting progress, what information
exists, what the tools can measure, how much a result costs, and what decision
the result must support.

The complete AI-assisted design system is the thing a team must engineer and
evaluate. It includes the people, methods, represented design state, tools,
checks, records, and decision authority that turn a design question into an
action. A bounded architecture study is one useful unit of work within that
system. It connects a specific question to permitted changes, tools,
measurements, comparisons, and a decision or honest stop. When a returned
result changes the recorded state and leads to another permitted action, the
study exhibits a design loop. @fig-arch2-loop shows that relationship. A study
may also close after one pass. The system, study, and loop support the book's
argument; none requires every project to follow one fixed sequence.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

system supplies people and authority, represented state, methods, environments
and tools, checks, and records to multiple bounded studies. One study may revise
an earlier request when a result supports another permitted action, or it may
close after one pass.](images/arch2-loop-diagram){#fig-arch2-loop width="100%"
fig-alt="Nested diagram in which a complete AI-assisted design system contains
persistent capabilities and multiple bounded architecture studies. One study
connects its question and scope to a work request, tool results, and a decision
or honest stop, with an optional revision arrow and a separate one-pass close."}
:::

Read @fig-arch2-loop from the outside inward. The outer boundary is the
persistent system a team must engineer. Its capabilities support more than one
study. The larger inner box follows one bounded question from scope to a work
request, tool results, and a decision or honest stop. The dashed return arrow is
optional; it applies only when a result supports another permitted action. The
line at the lower right shows the other valid case: a study can close after one
pass while the complete system remains available for later studies.

Machine learning has long optimized bounded mechanisms such as branch
prediction, scheduling, and placement. Newer systems can participate in a
larger share of design work, including problem formulation, artifact
generation, tool execution, result interpretation, and revision. The durable
question is not how autonomous the system appears. It is whether the complete
approach improves architecture work over a credible alternative at acceptable
total cost.

A useful result must still connect design intent to concrete alternatives,
alternatives to real tools, tool returns to qualified measurements,
measurements to an architecture conclusion, and that conclusion to an action
whose limits are clear.

## What This Book Teaches {.unnumbered}

The book is organized around one question. How should an architect use AI, if
at all, to improve system and chip design work? A reader who finishes the book
should be able to do the following work.

- Formulate the architecture question and the decision it must support.
- Diagnose which work is limiting progress before choosing a method.
- Represent the design state, relationships, permitted changes, and unknowns.
- Choose among conventional analysis, no AI, generation, prediction,
  optimization, or a small combination.
- Connect the chosen approach to real tools, reconstruct what ran, and
  determine which returns qualify as measurements.
- Compare the architecture result and the AI contribution separately against
  credible alternatives at comparable total cost.
- Explain what the result supports, decide what should happen next, and identify
  who is responsible for that action.

@sec-architecture-20-ontology introduces a useful default sequence for one
architecture study. The sequence helps teams separate questions that need different
outputs and checks. It is not a universal recipe, and the book does not require
every project to perform every stage in one order.

The distinction matters because system and chip design are not ordinary
classification tasks. The answer must survive interfaces, tools, workloads,
physical constraints, and verification. Some software errors can be patched
after deployment. An interface error or incorrectly implemented connection may
require a new hardware stepping or product revision once it is fixed in silicon
[@Intel2014CoreMIOUpdate]. AI can make candidate production cheaper without
making simulation, physical implementation, verification, or expert review
cheap. Faster production can therefore increase the work needed to determine
what those candidates actually do.

The continuous running case is the "Lighthouse prompt," a highly constrained
3\ W RISC-V extended reality (XR) subsystem. An XR headset concentrates the
cross-layer constraints the book must handle. Its power, thermal, and
performance limits interact tightly, and intuition can mispredict their joint
effect [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench; @HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. @sec-moonshot fixes the
long-term challenge. Later chapters return to it only when it gives a concrete
setting for the chapter's distinct question. The worked study in
@sec-running-the-loop is deliberately narrower. It shows what current tools
and measurements establish rather than pretending to complete the moonshot.

Computer architecture has absorbed major waves of automation before. Logic
synthesis became useful alongside timing analysis, equivalence checking, and
signoff practices that could expose an invalid result. AI-assisted work needs
the same engineering instinct. Fluent output, a completed tool run, and a
better score are not interchangeable with a supported architecture conclusion.

Architecture 2.0 remains computer architecture. The design question and the
standard of judgment stay architectural. The book draws on established methods
from adjacent fields because AI-assisted studies combine noisy estimates,
expensive experiments, evolving design state, and tools whose failures may not
be obvious.

| **Field** | **What it contributes** | **The failure it catches** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Experimental science | Falsifiable claims and planned tests | Rationalizing whatever the search happened to return |
| Statistics and decision science | Uncertainty estimates, surrogate prediction, and caution after selecting the best noisy result | Trusting the best of many noisy scores |
| Systems safety | Structured safety arguments and explicit decision authority | No one owning a consequential action |
| Benchmarking | Known inputs, comparable runs, and resistance to proxy gaming | Results that cannot be compared or reproduced |
| Software engineering | Regression testing, continuous integration, code review, version control | Silently breaking what already worked |
| Control theory | State estimation from noisy measurements | Mistaking a multi-fidelity reading for the post-layout truth |

: **Established disciplines contribute methods for specific problems in AI-assisted architecture work.** The synthesis lies in knowing when each method is needed and how it changes an architecture decision. {#tbl-borrowed-disciplines tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

Electronic design automation belongs at the center of this argument rather
than in @tbl-borrowed-disciplines. EDA tools connect architecture intent to
implementation and physical constraints. They may be stateful, depend on
proprietary inputs and process models, take hours or days to run, and return
failures as well as measurements. A small upstream change can cause downstream
routing, timing, power, or design-rule problems. Expensive tool work makes
prediction and search attractive, while the same complexity makes their
results difficult to trust without direct checks.

![**Architecture 2.0 connects three established fields.** Computer architecture supplies the questions and design tradeoffs, machine learning supplies methods for learning and search, and EDA supplies executable tools and physical measurements. Work at their intersection must satisfy the relevant standards of all three.](images/fig-book-composition){#fig-book-composition width="88%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation, with Architecture 2.0 at their intersection"}

This book places each borrowed idea where it helps answer an architecture
question inside the intersection in @fig-book-composition. The aim is
checkable engineering work rather than merely plausible output.

Using AI changes what teams must retain and what reviewers must inspect.
Workload traces, design artifacts, and tool outputs still matter. Problem
formulations, interface assumptions, experiment choices, tested explanations,
and serious alternatives also matter. A final design cannot show by itself why
the team reached its conclusion. A complete activity log is equally
insufficient when it lacks an architecture question or a supported explanation.

The book therefore focuses on durable engineering questions rather than
particular AI products. It does not propose replacing architects, EDA,
verification, or compiler engineering with a general AI layer. It does not
give a model authority merely because it produced a plausible artifact.
Architecture work still requires domain expertise, hard constraints, and
physical measurements. Named people remain responsible for the question, the
decision, and the conditions under which a recommendation applies.


## Book Structure {.unnumbered}

This lecture begins where the Architecture 2.0 foundations article
[@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20] ends. That article states the vision,
history, and capability horizons. This book develops a way to reason about
using AI across actual system and chip design work.

This is a focused synthesis rather than an encyclopedia, tool catalog, or
step-by-step handbook. Quantitative architecture texts remain the authority on
processor and memory tradeoffs [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach].
Machine-learning and EDA literature develop particular methods and tools. This
book asks how an architect should combine those bodies of knowledge without
losing the design question, physical meaning, empirical limits, or ownership
of the resulting action.

The chapters build one cumulative argument.

1. @sec-moonshot fixes an ambitious system-and-chip challenge and distinguishes
   a candidate from a useful result, bounded progress from full success, and a
   good design from proof that AI improved the work.
2. @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales shows why architecture work is becoming
   harder to finish and teaches readers to diagnose the work that is limiting
   a real decision.
3. @sec-architecture-20-ontology structures a separate technical comparison in
   the same project context as an architecture study with an intended decision,
   scope, budget, comparisons, and stopping conditions.
4. @sec-data-representations-world-models asks what data, relationships,
   history, permitted changes, and unknowns a method must be able to see.
5. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization selects among conventional
   analysis, no AI, generation, prediction, optimization, and small
   combinations.
6. @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces connects the selected
   approach to real tools while preserving state, conditions, failures, cost,
   and result identity.
7. @sec-feedback-verification-trust determines what a tool return means, what
   checks it passed, and which architecture claim it can support.
8. @sec-running-the-loop records the prospective cache study as not run rather
   than inventing a result, then completes a separate study whose inputs, tool
   path, and raw results can be inspected. Its outcome includes a failed
   explanation and a recommendation that remains pending.
9. @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack adapts the work to a new implementation
   decision rather than assuming that the earlier result transfers.
10. @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect evaluates the complete AI-assisted design
    system against a credible alternative at total cost, separates architecture
    outcome from AI contribution, and tests how the system fails.
11. @sec-what-architect-owns decides whether the architecture can be committed
    and states what architects and organizations remain responsible for.

The lifecycle in @sec-architecture-20-ontology, the Lighthouse example, and the
cumulative study record connect these chapters. Each is a supporting device.
The subject is how to think clearly about AI for system and chip design.

## Who This Book Is For {.unnumbered}

The primary audience is the computer architect. The book assumes enough
fluency to follow performance, energy, area, and software-interface tradeoffs
and to read an architecture paper, simulator, workload, or design report. It
does not assume a machine-learning background. The AI ideas needed for the
argument are introduced in an architecture setting.

The intersection in @fig-book-composition also gives the book four useful
entry points.

![**One book, four entry points.** Domain expertise and reader role place AI strategists, chief architects, ML researchers, and computer architects in different parts of the problem. Each can follow a different route through the chapters.](images/audience-quadrant){#fig-audience-quadrant width="100%" fig-alt="A 2x2 quadrant mapping AI Strategist, Chief Architect, ML Researcher, and Computer Architect across domain expertise and reader role"}

The four readers in @fig-audience-quadrant approach the material with
different goals.

- **The AI strategist** learns why architecture questions, physical limits,
  method choice, and complete-system evaluation constrain what AI can usefully
  contribute (@sec-moonshot, @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales,
  @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).
- **The ML researcher** learns how architecture state is represented, how EDA
  tools produce measurements, and why support limits and total comparison cost
  matter (@sec-data-representations-world-models,
  @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces,
  @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect).
- **The computer architect**, the primary reader, learns the full reasoning
  sequence from problem diagnosis through method choice, tool execution,
  interpretation, transfer, and commitment (@sec-architecture-20-ontology,
  @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-running-the-loop,
  @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack).
- **The chief architect** learns how to evaluate the complete approach, decide
  whether evidence is sufficient for commitment, and assign responsibility for
  the resulting action (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect,
  @sec-what-architect-owns).

Each reader enters from a different part of the problem. The shared test of
success is whether the reader can apply the reasoning to a problem other than
the Lighthouse.

## How to Read This Book {.unnumbered}

Each chapter opens with a guiding question and learning outcomes. The
Lighthouse request is a recurring anchor, but each return must perform a
different job. The worked study becomes the empirical anchor once the book has
established the representation, method choice, tool path, and interpretation
needed to understand it.

When the text depicts an agent, treat it as a bounded automated component
rather than a claim about human-level autonomy. Its name matters less than the
architecture work it may perform, the tools it may use, and the checks its
outputs must pass.

A fast orientation route includes the Preface, @sec-moonshot, and
@sec-what-architect-owns. The full argument reads the chapters in order.
Readers entering from one of the four roles in @fig-audience-quadrant can use
the cited chapters as a shorter route before returning to the full sequence.

In a graduate seminar, the chapter sequence supplies the conceptual spine.
The replay package behind @sec-running-the-loop can serve as the lab, and the
reviewer checklist in @sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist can support critique.
A student team can then apply the reasoning to one bounded architecture problem
of its own choosing. The point is not to imitate the book's example. It is to
show that the team can formulate, execute, evaluate, and decide within the
limits of a different problem.

Readers seeking hands-on practice should replay the worked study in
@sec-running-the-loop using the same package. Readers applying the approach to
a new problem should declare its limits and prepare a study brief, method
rationale, tool path, evaluation packet, tested explanation, and decision memo
that states what the evidence does and does not support.

Parts of this book will age quickly, and it is worth saying which. Named
models, benchmark scores, and tool capabilities are calibration points for
when the book was written. The durable bet is on architecture problem
formulation, representation, method choice, tool discipline, credible
comparison, careful interpretation, complete-system evaluation, and
responsible commitment. A future reader should be able to replace the models
and tools without losing the reasoning.

We do not need to wait for a system that designs a computer from one sentence.
We can build the representations, datasets, environments, experiments, and
professional judgment needed to use AI well today. Architecture 2.0 gives
architects a way to decide where AI helps, where it does not, what a result
means, and what should happen next.

— *Vijay Janapa Reddi*
